Kithil care much more about their tattoos than their fashions, and as a result their clothing tends to be simple and straightforward, though some Kithil will echo some of the markings on their body as accents on their clothes, especially if they can have those details sewn in by nearby Arcturian or Ordani artisans. As most Kithil are Keth, it is common for them to wear transluscent veils over the face to hide some of their teeth, and the same fabric is sometimes used on Kithil clothing, providing a clearer view of that tattoos beneath the fabric.

Cuisine & Diet

The shared meal around the cookfire is a fundamental part of Kithil culture, but the emphasis in their cooking is on shared ingredients and the celebration of the act of cooking, not any particular ingredient or spice. Generally, Kithil favor simple base recipes that work well even as individual ingredients change, and that can be easily shared out of a single pot, like soups and stews. The Kithil expression "no two soups the same," which refers to the way that seemingly similar situations can unfold very differently, is taken from their belief that each individual meal is shaped not just by the food that is served but by who has gathered to share it.

Technology & Magic

Traditionally, Kithil generally practice lunar magic, shifting both the spells they use and the way that they approach magic as the moons change, using spells that draw on fire when @UUID[JournalEntry.emberCosmos00000.JournalEntryPage.LKptgmc56euSOb0G]{Ragen} is ascendant, for example, or spells that improve speed when @UUID[JournalEntry.emberCosmos00000.JournalEntryPage.smc0OuMxsxfcSdhR]{Aura} is on the rise. Similarly, it is seen as lucky to begin projects that seem more resonant with a particular moon when that moon is dominant, sowing seeds during @UUID[JournalEntry.emberCosmos00000.JournalEntryPage.RkdBtFQk7STvMbV2]{Mayis} in the hopes of rain and building new structures under @UUID[JournalEntry.emberCosmos00000.JournalEntryPage.5pD8lxiilJJXOgoa]{Cora} to give them strength. The association between activities and the moons can be different from village to village, but they reflect a general belief that being flexible and changing activities is wise, with many Kithil learning a little bit about everything from smithing to repairing clothing to herbalism so that nothing is lost if disaster strikes unexpectedly.

Social Structure & Government

No matter how large they become, Kithil settlements are always known as villages. These settlements generally spread outwards across the land as opposed to building up as a city might, with individual Kithil and small groups living in stilted buildings around a central cookfire, protected from wild animals or natural dangers. Often, these buildings have elaborate window slats and shades that shut out Lantyr's light during the day, but allow the moonlight to come into each home at night. Kithil prefer using moonlight to candlelight or magical light where possible, and their windows are designed to allow enough light in to see and work by even on more overcast nights, though they will use other sources of illumination during times of truly inclement weather.

Within a village, groups of homes center around a cookfire, shared by a group that works together on tending crops and hunting. Cookfires generally use consensus to make major decisions, but cookfires are fluid, with individuals moving from one to another as fits their needs. Whoever comes to a cookfire is generally welcomed as long as they have no harmful intent towards those they are sharing food and time with, and any decisions that need to be made about what to do next are made by whoever is at the cookfire when a topic is raised, no matter how new they might be to the group.

Language & Communication

Kithil speak the language Mithia, as well as the Common Coin, and usually know a smattering of Arcden due to trade with Arcturians in the Plateau. Whichever language they are speaking, the Kithil communication style is consensus oriented, and Kithil often check in verbally to make sure they are understood while speaking, especially when speaking to those from other cultures.
Kithil.scoverview: The Kithil are a secluded moon-worshiping culture comprised primarily of Keth who reside across the ocean to the north of Ordain. The Kithil are an offshoot of the ancient Shent culture, from whom they inherit a strong spiritual connection to the elemental moons of Ember. Kithil traditions and culture are closely attuned to the orbital cycles of bodies in Ember’s cosmos. Many Kithil communities live nocturnal lifestyles, and most Kithil inscribe luminous tattoos onto their bodies, adding increasingly complex designs as they age. Kithil do not build large cities, preferring to distribute their society across many villages, with a practical focus on agriculture and communal bonds through cooking and shared meals.

Lumek.name: Lumek
Lumek.text:
At a Glance

  • Language: [[/language luma]]

  • Captial City: @UUID[JournalEntry.xqx0clu8pT4kRxAz.JournalEntryPage.654Xgg23ULcG04bO]{Hearth}

  • Technology: Iron/@UUID[Item.L1TdyHNyomGh8H3I]{Lumarin Steel} production, enhanced with fire magic.

  • Major Religions/Beliefs:@UUID[JournalEntry.emberDeities0000.JournalEntryPage.w5XsGfNsSEJnr1yd]{ Lumé}.

  • Names: Astarte, Lya, Lyax, Lucentis, Luna, Soluna, Lyra, Lyros, Thrax, Thala, Enki, Enja, Enjarr, Enya, Enyax, Ishtar, Ishtariak, Isha, Ishka, Iskar, Iskarrion, Lafa, Lafar, Ereshar, Eshkur, Kasha, Kashar.

  • Ancestries: [[/ancestry emberFej]] (80%) + (Other @UUID[JournalEntry.emberAncestries0.JournalEntryPage.yc1bRBrDsyaIi2C6]{Ancestries} exist in small numbers)

Wardens of Flame

The Lumek live under the oppressive cloud of constant survival, with unimaginable pressure to contain one of the world's greatest evils. They have been locked in a desperate fight against a remorseless and cruel enemy for centuries, and it has shaped their way of life and thinking to a degree that many other peoples of the world find hard to understand. When the Moiran people to their north began to fall, and the @UUID[JournalEntry.emberCultures000.JournalEntryPage.ZMHd8i0tOkhfOiKK]{Blood Barons} emerged, the Lumek were stirred into action and resistance by @UUID[JournalEntry.emberDeities0000.JournalEntryPage.w5XsGfNsSEJnr1yd]{Lumé}, the daughter of Naor, and since then, they have fought in the cycles of Fire & Death that many accept will one day overwhelm them.

The Lumek are constantly on guard against the undead to their north, but every decade or so, typically eleven years, the @UUID[JournalEntry.emberCultures000.JournalEntryPage.ZMHd8i0tOkhfOiKK]{Blood Barons} launch an all-out attack southwards that can last for months. These seemingly never-ending attacks are called the cycles of Fire & Death. The fighting is brutal; thousands die, outposts and fortifications are overrun, second, third, and fourth lines of defense are penetrated, and the resolve and morale of the defenders falter as the Lumek are forced back again and again. The only shining light amidst the chaos and death is Lumé herself. Charging between the lines, annihilating lesser undead, and clashing furiously with greater undead monsters without respite. Faith and religious fanaticism in Lumé, and in her ability to defend and keep their people safe, is therefore absolutely justified. Most of the Lumek see Lumé as a savior and a figure of total adoration that is only marred by ancient rumors of her mother's murder.

Daily life is often dominated by hard training, drills, and the ever-present air of coming doom. Despite the hardships, however, daily life for the Lumek is vibrant and ever-moving; their cities and settlements are always considered bustling, where the people go about their day with grace, speed, and an undercurrent of artistry.

Related Cultures

The Lumek are in a never-ending cycle of war with the @UUID[JournalEntry.emberCultures000.JournalEntryPage.ZMHd8i0tOkhfOiKK]{Blood Barons} and their undead hordes to their north. They are so focused on this fight that they rarely travel outside their borders unless rumors of undeath surface. However, they have good relations with all other cultures around them, even the @UUID[JournalEntry.emberCultures000.JournalEntryPage.bG3kuSiwqMnIHSrH]{Tayan Empire} whose technology and military might are extremely interesting to the Lumek.

Customs and Traditions

The Lumek are a dualistic culture in many ways; outsiders often gain very different insights into how the Lumek truly feel, depending on whether they are currently at war, approaching a conflict, or recovering from a recent struggle against the undead. That said, the Lumek are happy to share their cultural practices and traditions with outsiders, but they tend to be less interested in incorporating outside ideas. They efficiently manage their duties and are always aware of how long certain tasks take, knowing that war and conflict may loom just over the horizon. Gathering around a fire is a central aspect of Lumek daily life, serving both as a means to cook meals and as a space for relaxation and community bonding. It is traditional for Lumek households to be centered around a Firekep, a large, beautifully constructed fireplace made of metal and finely carved stones, often adorned with intricate designs that tell the family’s history. Celebrations for births are initiated quickly, as newborns are considered pivotal to the survival of their culture and the Lumek value large families, seeing each new life as a vital contribution to their collective strength and ability to endure the cycles of Fire & Death. The Lumek always burn their dead shortly after passing, with swift blessings and ceremonies. They do not maintain graveyards of any kind, as they believe that the spirits of the deceased are best honored through fire and are deathly afraid of the undead arising within their communities.

Every time the Blood Barons relent and the undead either retreat or are vanquished, the Lumek embrace a time of jubilant celebration that stretches over several weeks. For them, fire symbolizes not just a weapon but an ode to life itself. Their grand festivals become a vibrant display of this belief, showcasing fire in countless forms. Enormous bonfires leap towards the sky, handheld sparks flicker and dance in the air, while skilled performers breathe flames and twirl fiery instruments with graceful abandon. Accompanied by the resounding beat of great drums, songs of triumph and joy fill the air, creating an atmosphere of unrivaled merrymaking. This unique period allows the Lumek to mend their wounded spirits, embracing the warmth and energy of the flames as they revel in renewal and hope.

Religion & Beliefs

The Lumek view themselves as fighters and warriors by necessity. When it comes to their personal hopes and dreams, the vast majority would like nothing more than to live simple lives and practice art, music, and dance. This view makes them extremely dutiful, and they recognize that their sacrifice keeps the world safe, even if they suffer. This sometimes presents itself as dry, fatalistic humor, among others, and deeply held cynicism regarding the fate of the world and the purpose of all things. Still, Lumek can also be beacons of positivity as they express themselves fully with the time they have.

In times of conflict, the clerics, direct followers and champions of @UUID[JournalEntry.emberDeities0000.JournalEntryPage.w5XsGfNsSEJnr1yd]{Lumé} channel their divine and elemental powers to protect their people and repel invaders, often invoking the blessings of Lumé to enhance their abilities. In daily life, they use their powers to heal, bless crops, and maintain harmony within the community. The rituals performed by these clerics often involve offerings to Lumé and elaborate ceremonies that celebrate her protective nature and the elemental force of fire.

Clothing & Adornments

Lumek clothing is a blend of practicality and artistry, featuring hardy, resilient forms alongside refined and beautifully crafted pieces with flowing shapes. The color palette frequently includes striking reds and blacks, with many Lumek embellishing their attire with @UUID[Item.L1TdyHNyomGh8H3I]{Lumarin Steel} charms believed to protect against undeath, disease, and ill health.

While most inhabitants of the Firelands do not wear armor on a daily basis, they all possess defensive clothing and weaponry, often keeping these items close at hand in case fighting breaks out. During their festivals at the beginning of a new cycle after the defeat of a Blood Baron attack, Lumek wear special celebration attire. These festival garments are much lighter and less practical, allowing for greater freedom of movement when dancing. They often feature an array of decorative elements, including gemstones, precious metal adornments, and beautiful charms.

Cuisine & Diet

Lumek cuisine revolves around a common dish called Luksa, a broad term for a mixture of dense grains, meats, and a specific pungent spice blend. Luksa is easy to prepare, and different Lumek communities have their own versions of the dish, utilizing locally available ingredients. All the spices in Luksa are sourced from plantations and farms across the Lumek Homelands, known for their aromatic and extremely spicy qualities; most other ancestries cannot eat Luksa unless it has been toned down significantly for them. Given that the Lumek culture primarily consists of the @UUID[JournalEntry.emberAncestries0.JournalEntryPage.fmhP7pxXIXV0BM2r]{Fej }Ancestry, their food and cuisine are notably nutrient-dense and high in calories. They also tend to serve large portions, and when not engaged in defending the Firelands, they heartily indulge in lavish feasts.

Technology & Magic

In addition to their fighting prowess taught to them through necessity and hard training, the Lumek are master blacksmiths. Most of their technology revolves around a unique process where the ashes of their dead are used to create weapons and armour, known as @UUID[Item.L1TdyHNyomGh8H3I]{Lumarin Steel}. A rare metal that is considered holy and typically not allowed to leave the Firelands' shores unless permitted by Lumé herself. Lumarin Steel comes in several different grades, and it is rumored that the ashes of the more faithful defenders and champions imbue the metal with power, making them stronger and giving them both the ability to cause more damage to undead but also enhance the fighting abilities of its wielder. It should come as no surprise then that the Lumek burn their dead in holy ceremonies to collect thier ashes and use them in the fighting to come.

There are three major blacksmithing institutions across the Firelands, each with a specific focus. These schools teach incredibly ancient and traditional crafting processes. The three schools are the Vanbrel, which teaches weapon crafting and aggressive weapons of war; the Julmea, which teaches armorsmithing and defense construction techniques; and finally the Farimer, which teaches practical technologies for crafting everyday items used in farming or industry.

As for magic, the Lumek do not have any formal schools or academies for teaching or studying the arcane. Their understanding of magic is deeply rooted in their cultural practices and traditions rather than structured education. They are generally open to various forms of magical practices introduced by visitors. However, the Lumek place a high value on magic users who possess innate or ancestral connections to elemental forces, particularly those that resonate with fire or the elemental moon of @UUID[JournalEntry.emberCosmos00000.JournalEntryPage.LKptgmc56euSOb0G]{Ragen} itself. Any magical connection to fire is seen as a mark of honor and respect, and those who can harness these gifts are often revered within their communities. Many Lumek who wield magic are also priests and clerics of Lumé. Her followers play a crucial role in both warfare and everyday life.

Social Structure & Government

The Lumek are governed by their queen and ultimate ruler, the Shard Goddess @UUID[JournalEntry.emberDeities0000.JournalEntryPage.w5XsGfNsSEJnr1yd]{Lumé}. There is a profound level of devotion, fanaticism, and faith in her ability to keep them safe, with everyone doing everything possible to contribute to the war against the undead. In turn, Lumé rules with absolute power across the entire realm but delegates much of the day-to-day governance to city leaders who are elected after every Cycle of Fire & Death, or to local leaders who tend to retain their position based on ability, age, or a combination of both. They oversee daily operations and administration, ensuring that resources are allocated effectively for essential activities such as farming and defense. This involves organizing and training individuals to be sent to the front lines or forming volunteer groups to prepare citizens for their roles in the ongoing conflict against the undead. To outsiders, it may seem strange at first, but there is very little variance in social classes, and groups are not treated differently. For example, there is no special respect or acknowledgment for warriors or those who have fought on the front lines. This is because everyone believes that all members of Lumek culture have a duty to fight or support their efforts, and whether you are fighting or farming, you should still be honored for your sacrifice.

language & Communication

The Lumek language is called Luma and is a very fast, easy-to-learn spoken tongue with a level of depth and complexity that can take a lifetime to master. There are very few long words but many short expressive words and phrases; for example, the Lumek has nearly 80 different words to describe fire.
Lumek.scoverview: The Lumek dwell upon the rust-colored mountains and barren shores of the Firelands, located southwest of Ordain across the Yawning Sea. They are personally led and protected by the fire goddess Lumé, who helps them resist the dark forces of undeath. Years of continuous warfare against the Blood Barons and Lumé's direct guidance have shaped the Lumek military into one of the most formidable in the entire world. The Lumek have a fearsome reputation as unyielding warriors with a penchant for stoicism and cynical humor. They also harbor a love of art, celebration, and dance, which manifests in lavish festivals during occasional periods of respite from war.

Strider.name: Strider
Strider.text:
At a Glance

  • Language: [[/language forest]]

  • Captial City: @UUID[JournalEntry.xqx0clu8pT4kRxAz.JournalEntryPage.USnD05PQDlKzGowb]{Sirewood}

  • Technology: Symbiotic with nature, enhanced with Druidic magic.

  • Major Religions/Beliefs: Primalism, Wild Gods

  • Names: Baul, Bhun, Brood, Draig, Drunn, Gholt, Glaw, Gnash, Grak, Grend, Jarg, Khul, Knaw, Krane, Morn, Murk, Nyrauk, Rakaar, Rask, Rhogar, Sin, Skar, Skorn, Skraal, Skun, Slog, Thrag, Thul, Vang, Varr

  • Ancestries: [[/ancestry emberKeth]] (85%) + [[/ancestry emberHuman]] (5%), [[/ancestry emberThornling]] (5%) (Other @UUID[JournalEntry.emberAncestries0.JournalEntryPage.yc1bRBrDsyaIi2C6]{Ancestries} exist in small numbers)

Growth and Decay

The Striders of the Corebright Forest are a hardy people deeply connected to nature, living in harmony with the natural world. They dwell among the treetops of colossal Elderbark trees, residing high in the canopy or within massive trunk villages, isolated from the outside world. They have little concept of progress, choosing instead to live exsist in a state of symbiosis with the trees, plants, animals, and monsters that surround them. Since the Corebright is a wild and untamed region, it is no surprise that many Wild Gods and Leviathans reside there, and the Striders not only worship these beings but have also become increasingly intertwined with the ecosystems they oversee. These local entities embody specific domains, such as the "Lord of the Sun-Dappled Ferns" or the "Matriarch of the Deep Roots and are treated as active, present neighbors whose favor is courted through the maintenance of their specific territories.

Despite this outward harmony, the Striders are often embroiled in internal schisms and conflicts between sects, factions, and groups, each holding different ideas about how nature should be interpreted. One faction might worship a Wild God that exemplifies the strength and beauty of growth, while another may revere a Leviathan dwelling in the tangled root systems beneath the forest floor, following its example of embracing decay and rebirth. These disagreements often boil over into violence, and much like the natural world itself, striders are not above killing and attempting to supplant another group.

To the rest of the world, the Striders are barely noticed on the global stage. They stay hidden in the forest unless they feel threatened. Some neighboring nations, like the Tayan Empire, do not recognize strict borders around the Striders—instead viewing the Corebright Forest as both a threat to control, via the Kirargy Knights, and a resource to exploit. Recently, Osscarhate has made several attempts to attack and clear the forest edges near their territory, even sending armies into the trees to wipe out the Striders and kill as many Wild Gods and levthians as possible. However, these actions did not end well for the Blood Barons and demonstrated to the world that the Striders can unite against a common threat, as seen when they annihilated the undead host that entered the Corebright.

Related Cultures

The Corebright Forest directly touches upon three other cultures, the Tayan Empire in the west, the Blood Barons in the south, and the Cascilian Republic in the southeast. The Tayan Empire doesn't consider the Strider culture to be a threat in any way and treats the Corebright Forest as something they will eventually control through slow expansion and clearing of its trees. The Striders are somewhat fearful of the Tayan Empire, however, and make few efforts to oppose them. The Blood Barons cannot expand into the Corebright Forest effectively due to its overwhelming scale, the ferocity of its creatures, and the lack of denser populations to replenish its numbers; thus, the Blood Barons and the Striders ignore one another. The Cascilians and the Stiders have very good relationships, and the Casilians turn a blind eye to the Druidic magic practiced by the Striders in return for lucrative trade deals.
Strider.scoverview: The Striders of the Corebright Forest live beneath towering Elderbark trees that cover a colossal expanse at the center of the Aterican continent. Most of the culture is composed of Keth who fled the Shana Mountains to their east during the Shattering although in recent centuries more and more humans belong to their communities. For the most part, the Striders live in harmony with each other and with the omnipresent natural power of the forest, but not all Strider communities agree and there are notable off-shoots that foment particularly vehement disagreement or violent conflict.

Tayan.name: Tayan
Tayan.text:
At a Glance

  • Language: [[/language imperial]]

  • Great City: @UUID[JournalEntry.xqx0clu8pT4kRxAz.JournalEntryPage.7iZDVtrBO7326XZY]{Caren'ac}

  • Technology: Aethyra, Iron/Steel production, enhanced with munitions development

  • Major Religions/Beliefs: @UUID[JournalEntry.emberDeities0000.JournalEntryPage.SXks9PsVzNyIPuDH]{Tanir}

  • Names: Aethelx, Aelric, Alfwyn, Bear, Born, Baelmorn, Brith, Cynric, Ceol, Cynefyr, Drax, Eadric, Eofor, Guth, Scalos, Gorm, Hrothgar, Hyge, Icaen, Kyn, Krag, Lorica, Loris, Osrica, Oswald, Orm, Siglrum, Sunder, Stith, Wulfe, Wuam.

  • Ancestries: [[/ancestry emberHuman]] (75%) + [[/ancestry emberDrakon]] (5%) (Other @UUID[JournalEntry.emberAncestries0.JournalEntryPage.yc1bRBrDsyaIi2C6]{Ancestries} exist in small numbers)

Manifest Imperialism

The Tayan Empire is a vast and fiercely expansionist state that dominates the western known @UUID[JournalEntry.emberCosmos00000.JournalEntryPage.9aUFzpVzfkJ1UIZX]{world of Ember's} surface. Through a combination of military might, political cunning, and industrial innovation, the Tayan armies have spread to distant corners of the continent of @UUID[JournalEntry.xqx0clu8pT4kRxAz.JournalEntryPage.UXitezaq69A5JVmd]{Aterica}. Born from the fractured Northern Carawn Kingdoms seventy years ago during an event known as the @UUID[JournalEntry.umX2Xt1eMUC0ECgc.JournalEntryPage.Fze49xRKzbsO5qNq]{Night of Swords} in the great city of @UUID[JournalEntry.xqx0clu8pT4kRxAz.JournalEntryPage.7iZDVtrBO7326XZY]{Caren’ac}, the city has become the heart of centralized authority. Caren’ac is a testament to the empire’s power, a gleaming metropolis built around a series of concentric lakes. Its towering spires are now crisscrossed with Aeth-Pipes, where red-vapor lamps glow in the dusk, and the constant hum of mechanized industry fills the air.

The rise of the Tayan Empire across the region was swift and often brutal, driven by a doctrine of Manifest Destiny that claimed the Tayan Empire as the preeminent vanguard against the world’s greatest evils, including undeath and monsters. Its armies are spread across multiple fronts: the 2nd Army battles the @UUID[JournalEntry.emberCultures000.JournalEntryPage.SySGCB7QdgeKowkD]{Kelmezian} City State Alliance, the 3rd campaigns against the @UUID[JournalEntry.emberCultures000.JournalEntryPage.cYMQIQFugpO79L9f]{Mazira} Kingdoms across the @UUID[JournalEntry.xqx0clu8pT4kRxAz.JournalEntryPage.AZTOp0G5w0lKUHfL]{Crossing Sea}, the 4th presses north against the vicious Skitari, and the 6th, newly formed, trains in secrecy, its first deployment a closely guarded mystery.

Society within the empire is tightly controlled, with the Empress slowly curbing the power of certain great noble houses that once dominated the empire's cities. Through the erosion of Founded Rights, arranged marriages, engineered debts, and public trials often executed by the fearsome Vyrn, formally known as the Directorate, these families are culled or absorbed, their influence reduced as the empire consolidates control over Aethyra production and key industrial resources. The @UUID[JournalEntry.emberOrganizatio.JournalEntryPage.Qd6EE6pvR97O1OmH]{Kirargy Knights}, once the pinnacle of honor and defenders of law, now find themselves increasingly sidelined; some serve the empire directly, commanding armies or guarding cities, while others struggle to maintain relevance in a world reshaped by Aethyric machines.

Central to the empire’s transformation is Aethyra, a volatile alchemical liquid distilled from sulfur, Metizol, and Lithite. Stable until activated with small rods of Lithite, it produces either a red-orange steam or a devastating explosive force, depending on the purity of Lithite, powering everything from urban infrastructure and machinery to experimental rifles, Munitions, armored warframes, and massive mobile siege engines. The cities themselves pulse with emerging uses of Aethyra, steam and vapor rising from the more populous cities with industries now humming day and night, creating a rhythmic industrial heartbeat.

Related Cultures

The Tayan Empire is at open war with two neighboring cultures: the Kelmezians to the south and the Maziran Kingdoms across the sea to the west. Their expansionist ambitions have given them a terrible reputation among most of the more distant cultures; however, the Lumek are impressed with their technological progress and have been happy in recent years to host a Tayan-funded military enclave within their borders. The Striders to their east are mostly ignored, although the slow destruction and clearing of the massive Corebright Forest by the Tayan Empire is taking its toll on relations.

Life in the Tayan Empire is both vibrant and perilous: citizens enjoy unprecedented convenience in illuminated streets, mechanized workshops, and public bathhouses, but loyalty is demanded, and the shadow of the Vyrn ensures that freedom carries a constant risk. The air smells faintly of sulfur and metal, the streets hiss with pressurized vapor, and the red-orange glow of Aethyric lamps bathes every corner, serving as a reminder of the empire’s power, its progress, and the ever-present eye of the Empress.

Customs and Traditions

The Tayan Empire is still a relatively young nation, and as such lacks a unified cultural identity. The Empire is a patchwork of traditions inherited from the many city-states, clans, and territories of the Northern Carawn Kingdoms that were unified under the Imperial banner. Each major city and its surrounding regions retain their own distinct customs, festivals, and social expectations, creating a cultural landscape that is as varied as it is vibrant. Over time, the Tayans have become known for a general reverence for order, personal honour, and civic participation, values championed by the Empress and woven into public life. Whether through local festivals, commemorations of unification, or the everyday rituals of hospitality and respect.

Some cities honor ancient seasonal rites, such as lighting sky lanterns over the Restless Bay or creating small markers as offerings to nature spirits, among the northern cities surrounded by the Vanthar Forest. As time has passed, many of the larger and more developed cities, especially those closer to the heartland, have begun developing new, distinctly Tayan traditions, from the Swords Day Festival to the formalized religious ceremonies under the Three Temples that have elevated within the Empire and the pilgrimages to the Temple complexes themselves where the three main @UUID[JournalEntry.emberDeities0000.JournalEntryPage.6pJu6l3a7RTzcaRM]{Shard Gods} of the Empire reside personally. While the Empire also publicly encourages local practices, some are seen as problematic and have been gradually eliminated over the years; however, overall, the Empire views its vast cultural differences as a strength.

Religion & Beliefs

Culturally, the citizens of the Tyana empire follow the pantheon of the Tanir, which includes deities more closely associated with their political enemies, such as Malae or Fenra Irdragon. Officially, the Empire's view on religion is to turn a blind eye to these older beliefs, but unofficially, the Empress enacted a policy of Systematic Dissolution many years ago, a process that slowly encourages her citizens to worship only deities approved by the Empire. To that end, the Empire has three major temples, entire organizations dedicated to the worship of a single god. In the capital of Caren'ac, the Temple of Selai and her Court of Silver is the largest and most influential. Followed by Tirass in the city of Kawn and Zhaen in the city of Kayhurn. To Tayan citizens, their gods are not distant beings but are spiritual leaders and guides that anchor their daily lives and obedience to the laws of the Empire. Pilgrimages to these temples are common, and great processions are sometimes organized for the devout to travel safely from one city to another.

Clothing & Adornments

Tayan fashion prioritizes a cultural desire for "Refined Elegance," favoring structured silhouettes, high collars, and heavy fabrics like wool and treated leather that resist the oily residue of Aethyra vapor. This also gives the military an iconic mix of ancient knightly flair and modern practicality, with most of the empire's foot soldiers adorned in sharp, distinctive garments. The color palette is dominated by Imperial Crimson, Iron Grey, and deep black. Ordinary citizens wear simple clothing that mirrors this, reduced to basic shapes and ideas, while higher-ranking merchants and members of the bureaucracy wear clothing akin to uniforms, with Gorget-Pins or metallic badges that denote their civic rank. Members of the nobility who belong to the great houses try not to display their wealth and status, inlaying their coats and clothing with gold embroidery on the layers hidden from casual view. While the Tayan nobility try not to directly display their status, they wear decorative chains or embroidered ropes, subtly referencing their financial and political ties to the Empress.

Cuisine & Diet

Tayan food was once as varied as its people, but with the rise of the Empire and the resulting increased regional safety and security, and unrestricted trade, the population has experienced an unprecedented boom. This surge has created new challenges in food production and supply, especially in supplying its many vast armies. To address this, the empire cultivates large quantities of Iteper, a rapidly growing root crop that thrives almost everywhere, alongside extensive fields of wheat and fruit. As its industry developed, the empire also began producing large amounts of salt from huge mines and vinegar in large-scale factories, which helped preserve food and addressed the issue of widespread food procurement and delivery. A popular staple for workers is the "Caken Pasty," a dense, salt-cured meat-and-root-vegetable pie that can last several weeks on a shelf or in the back of a cart without losing flavor.

Technology & Magic

As the empire gradually formed, one of its most remarkable achievements was the discovery and production of Aethyra, an alchemical liquid made from sulfur, Metizol, and its catalyst component, Lithite. Nearly all of its technological advancements can be linked to Aethyra in some way. The Tayan Empire has had access to Aethyra for the last thirty years or so and has slowly begun to fully incorporate it into its military, through the use of powerful handheld explosives known as Aethyra Munitions. The Tayan military has also developed ranged weapons that fire bullets at high speed using the energy from these explosions, powered by Aethyra, but most are still experimental and reserved for elite troops. Aethyra has also become integrated into civilian life in major cities, sparking an industrial boom as the high-pressure steam generated by Aethyra reactions powers increasingly complex machinery. Aeth-pipes run beneath main streets, carrying pressurized vapor from central Crucible Houses to public baths, workshops, and lighting pylons. Workshops now operate continuous shifts thanks to reliable power from small Aeth-cells. Simple mechanization—lathes, looms, presses, and drills driven by pressure shafts—has become common. Noise and vibration now dominate the industrial districts, creating a rhythmic pulse that marks the workday.

Alongside this emerging technology, the Tayan Empire also maintains a strong tradition and a desire to continue using magic, which still plays a prominent role in its military. In fact, magic use remains commonplace within the empire, but it is gradually becoming a luxury reserved for nobility or the wealthy.

Social Structure & Government

To most, the Tayan Empire functions as a Centralized Autocracy, ruled officially by the Empress's will and desires, whose word is law. However, beneath the surface, it is a battleground for rival factions kept in check by her iron will and attention. When she is distracted or unable to monitor everything, issues can slip through the cracks. But the Empress is believed to have eyes everywhere, and she is almost unimaginably well-informed about events happening within the Empire and beyond its borders.

  • The Empress & The Vryn: At the heart of the Empire sits the Empress and her family, who rule not through consensus but through absolute power. While she allows governors to handle local affairs in her name, she maintains her authority through her personal enforcers known as the Vryn. This shadow organization acts as the Empire's iron fist of control, using engineered debts, public trials, and accidents to bankrupt and eliminate any noble Holds or political figures that oppose the Empire's goals.

  • The Mechanica: This newly formed organization is the true backbone of the Empire’s power and is led by none other than Lorgi himself. The Mechanica controls the distillation, transportation, and regulation of Aethyra. Since every factory, streetlamp, and munition requires Aethyra to function, the Mechanica holds a significant amount of influence over every other faction. They are quickly becoming the new age elite, often clashing with the old nobility, who see these engineers and alchemists as upstarts with greasy hands.

  • The Fading Noble Holds: Once sovereign rulers over cities and the sole noble class of the Northern Carawn Kingdoms, the Holds are now in a state of managed decay. Those who survived the Night of Swords and have fallen in line are allowed to keep their titles and estates only on the condition of complete loyalty. Their rights and privileges are being replaced by a slow and effective process of turning ancient lords into middle managers or displacing them entirely.

  • The Imperial Army: The largest and most favored branch, the Army is a juggernaut of military power, with massive armies comprising well-trained and efficient soldiers led by brilliant commanders hand-picked by the Empress.

  • The Imperial Navy: While the Army conquers the land, the Navy secures the Seas. They are often at odds with the Army for resources as they protect the vital trade routes that keep Caren’ac wealthy.

  • The Kirargy Knights: The Old Guard of the Empire, once the proud elite of Tayan society, remains highly influential. Many have joined the military as elite commanders, yet numerous traditionalists continue to strive to protect the people, battling monsters, even as they watch honor give way to expansion, brutality, and efficiency.

  • The Temples of the Shard Gods: The three main Temples serve as the moral and spiritual anchor that prevents the Empire from collapsing into civil war. Many Shard Gods publicly support the Empire, and their priesthoods have immense political leverage. The Empress must maintain a delicate balance with the Temples: appease their whims to a degree while curbing their influence.

Language & Communication

The name of the Empires offical language is Imperial. A precise, standardized language designed for efficiency and command based upon the older Arcden language and newer stranger words. It has replaced many local dialects to ensure the vast bureaucracy and military can function without friction.
Tayan.scoverview: Far to the west, beyond the near-endless Corebright Forest, lies the colossal Tayan Empire, the largest predominantly human nation on the surface of Ember. Ruled by the ambitious Dragon Empress, the Tayan empire is a powerful realm defined by relentless expansion, industrial might, and a society reshaped by the volatile alchemical substance Aethyra. Its cities hum with the ceaseless pulse of mechanized workshops and hissing pipes, bathed in the glow of Aethic lamps, while the streets and spires are overseen by the ever-present gaze of the Vryn, the Empress’s feared and secretive enforcers. Noble houses rise and fall under the careful orchestration of imperial politics, as old traditions clash with the demands of progress. The ancient order of the Kirargy Knights still holds positions of military and political clout, their presence a living reminder of the empire’s mythical power through their command of Dragons.

Maziran.name: Maziran
Maziran.text:
At a Glance

  • Language: [[/language kaziric]]

  • Great City: @UUID[JournalEntry.xqx0clu8pT4kRxAz.JournalEntryPage.iWPrQ1UOb32aZL1u]{Lunarai}

  • Technology: Steel production, enhanced with Earth magic, Steam Engines, Telescopes, and Skyriders.

  • Major Religions/Beliefs: @UUID[JournalEntry.emberDeities0000.JournalEntryPage.SXks9PsVzNyIPuDH]{The Tanir}, Bound Ancestors, Disdain for gods.

  • Names: Arazek, Aysera, Kaeril, Kareshi, Keirra, Korin, Korval, Maerik, Marashi, Raeshin, Ravel, Reshukan, Seruka, Shirok, Shyren, Taresk, Tashira, Taven, Vashari, Veyrok, Yoruko, Zenshi

  • Ancestries: [[/ancestry emberHuman]] (65%) + [[/ancestry emberCorak]] (20%) (Other @UUID[JournalEntry.emberAncestries0.JournalEntryPage.yc1bRBrDsyaIi2C6]{Ancestries} exist in small numbers).

Sky Devourers

Far beyond the distant Tayan Empire, in the furthest west of the known world, lie the Maziran Kingdoms, a fractured realm of mountain peaks, ancient fortresses, and unyielding pride. To most of the world, Mazira is little more than a myth, spoken of in tales of Skyriders, cities carved into the mountains, and endless wars. Even more feared are the seasonal Skyfalls, when the heavens are said to rain black water and swarms of terrifying monsters called Jagkat tear apart those foolish enough to step beyond the protection of fortress walls. These swarms descend in madness, ravaging villages, towns, and cities, with relentless hunger, and every Maziran grows up beneath their ever-present shadow.

Though the Mazirans of today are largely Human, their culture descends from a far older people, the Cor’ak, whose civilization carved its mark deep into the bones of @UUID[JournalEntry.xqx0clu8pT4kRxAz.JournalEntryPage.3ImHPBYTX7u3OqEQ]{Akazea} mountains. Mazirans define themselves through tradition, ancestry, and loyalty to their homeland. Ever'sy stone temple, stepped valley farm, and battle standard bears echoes of the Cor’ak legacy.

Yet for all their pride, the Mazirans are deeply divided. Their eight known kingdoms, with a whispered ninth said to lie beyond the western wastes, are locked in perpetual rivalry: warring, trading, and scheming in cycles as old as their history. Kingdoms rise and fall; alliances shift with the seasons. Only @UUID[JournalEntry.FYP2Af9bY4B9lSqi.JournalEntryPage.U1lERnH3iJ32wOMn]{Norzi Ashigurin}, the Shenin of Lunari and Lord of Storms, dares claim dominion over all Akazea, his banners reaching farther than any ruler for hundreds of years.

Maziran cities are dense and vertical, linked by tramways that climb cliffsides or hang suspended over vast chasms. While many industries have embraced full industrialization, traditional methods, slower, meticulous, and deeply valued, still hold an important place in Maziran society. Their craftsmanship is unmatched: metalwork, stone architecture, and magically-assisted mining flourish beneath the mountain peaks. Many Mazirans wield earth-attuned magic, shaping stone and ore through sheer will, carving their cities directly from the mountains themselves.

Among the proudest callings in Mazira is service in the Azeken, an ancient order of Skyriders who swear sacred oaths to the Shenins and the only ones who dare travel openly during a Skyfall. Each Azeken bonds with a winged mount called a Tekrel, a terrifying creature of Akazea’s high ranges. They serve out their contracts for a single season before returning home, free to offer their services to the highest bidder.

Related Cultures

The Maziran Kingdoms are united under a shared cultural identity, yet remain divided into multiple rival kingdoms, often engaged in open warfare with one another. In addition, the Mazirans are facing an external threat: the @UUID[JournalEntry.emberCultures000.JournalEntryPage.bG3kuSiwqMnIHSrH]{Tayan} Empire, which landed on their eastern shores nearly fifteen years ago. Since then, the Kingdom of Kanre has been subjugated. Surprisingly, the Mazirans appear relatively unfazed by the Tayan conquest and hold no particular animosity toward the Tayans. They maintain generally good relations with many neighboring cultures, including the @UUID[JournalEntry.emberCultures000.JournalEntryPage.SySGCB7QdgeKowkD]{Kelmezians}, who are currently attempting to rally the Mazirans to set aside their internal conflicts and unite against the Tayan threat.
Maziran.scoverview: The Marizan Kingdoms are an almost mythical culture that exists in the furthest lands of the world to the west, even beyond the distant Tayan Empire. A realm of jagged mountains and ancient fortresses, known to most only in tales of Skyriders, endless wars, and seasonal Skyfalls, when black rain and swarms of monsters called Jagkat descend upon the unprotected. Their vertical cities, connected by cliff-hanging tramways, blend unmatched craftsmanship and earth magic. The Azeken Skyriders, who bond with winged mounts called Tekrel, risk their lives and sanity in seasonal contracts, facing the horrors of Skyfalls and mastering the Devouring Sky to protect their people and uphold their personal honor, loyalty, and the fragile legacy of their mountain homes.
Maziran.sgamemaster: The Mazirans’ most closely guarded secret is that both the Jagkat swarms and their winged mounts, the Tekrel, are Abyssal entities. The Azeken bond with their mounts through unknown means, allowing them to control these creatures and even oppose the Jagkat, yet the nature of this control remains a mystery: some whisper it is ritual, others claim it is will or bloodline. This does not explain why Skyfalls occur, but it sheds light on why only the Azeken can defy the swarms, wielding powers as terrifying as the monsters they claim to destroy.

Waerd.name: Waerd
Waerd.text:
At a Glance

  • Language: [[/language wyrdic]]

  • Captial City: Split between @UUID[JournalEntry.xqx0clu8pT4kRxAz.JournalEntryPage.aMcq6g62RzqDF97Q]{Oshclaw}, @UUID[JournalEntry.xqx0clu8pT4kRxAz.JournalEntryPage.Pt3rDHmZDqfY6f9e]{Chimeras} and @UUID[JournalEntry.xqx0clu8pT4kRxAz.JournalEntryPage.P6TRMP4ZhskQVJXa]{Wick}.

  • Technology: Late bronze, early iron/steel production, enhanced with monster materials.

  • Major Religions/Beliefs: @UUID[JournalEntry.emberDeities0000.JournalEntryPage.J8wfDAZmky3f5VvV]{The Nineteen}. Specifically @UUID[JournalEntry.emberDeities0000.JournalEntryPage.6dEDqbOX2xuQLUgZ]{Lanespear}.

  • Names: Aato, Tauno, Samu, Laurila, Tatu, Ukko, Manne, Hannula, Jani, Valtonen, Arho, Riku, Joutsen, Emme, Marttila, Naimi, Rissanen, Leea, Hulda, Ahola, Vellamo, Kallio, Merja, Kreeta, Tekla, Karoliina

  • Ancestries: [[/ancestry emberHuman]] (45%) + [[/ancestry emberSignborn]](35%), [[/ancestry emberAshka]](10%) (Other @UUID[JournalEntry.emberAncestries0.JournalEntryPage.yc1bRBrDsyaIi2C6]{Ancestries} exist in small numbers)

Monster Slayers

The Waerds of the Lowlands are the world's foremost monster hunters, known for their relentless battles against creatures of the Duskflare Jungles and each other. They define themselves by their ability to defeat monsters and rivals. Six massive city-castles called Bastions dominate the Lowlands, where life centers on shifting alliances and skirmishes; long-term peace is almost unthinkable. Despite ongoing political conflicts, Waerds respect each other pragmatically; they follow strange codes of honor and rebuilding periods to prevent their wars from driving them to extinction. In these battles, death is rare, and victory is measured by individual courage and endurance rather than slaughter. For Waerds, fighting one another is simply a test or practice for the real challenge, heading into the jungles to slay monsters.

At the core of this philosophy of hunting and fighting is a deep reverence for @UUID[JournalEntry.emberDeities0000.JournalEntryPage.6dEDqbOX2xuQLUgZ]{Lanespear.} Her influence can be felt throughout the Lowlands, from fortified shrines overflowing with monster trophies to the elite companies of tattooed warrior-priests who bear spears in her honor. While Lanespear herself roams the Duskflare Jungles in search of colossal prey, she indirectly guides the Bastions by training members of all Waerds, no matter the political situation.

While the Waerd culture includes many humans, the true history of the subcontinent remains likely far more mysterious and strange. It is believed that a large, hidden population of Signborn inhabited the area for unknowable thousands of years, even during the long years of the Aedir Empire. After the Shattering, humans discovered the Lowlands, and eventually, the Signborn, and both Ancestries merged into a single, unified culture that exists today. This explains why Waerds have unique customs and traditions, such as viewing themselves as living chronicles rather than recording history on paper. They ritualistically tattoo their bodies throughout their lives to mark every successful hunt and significant battle. These intricate patterns serve as a visual history, with colors and styles varying by their Bastion of origin.

Their obsession with hunting monsters extends to armor and weaponry itself, as the Waerds specialize in biomimetic craftsmanship. They scavenge hide, bone, and essence from the creatures they slay, incorporating these materials into their armor and weapons to turn the monsters' strength against them. For a Waerd, a warrior’s worth is written in the ink on their skin and the jagged, runic trophies they wear into battle.

Related Cultures

The Waerds have strange relationships with surrounding nations and cultures, as the Waerds focus heavily on interior conflicts between themselves and fighting the monsters of their homeland. Most other cultures are simply disinterested in dealing with the Waerds and vice versa, so the majority of contact and connections are simply cordial. For example, there are no official embassies from any of the Waerd Bastions in Ordain, one of the largest trading cities nearby, though Ordani Trading Houses do have offices in several of the Waerd Bastions.

Customs & Tradition

Waerds live by a series of complex codes, often simply called "The Codes," as if everyone knows what they are. Ironically, to many Waerds, the codes they follow can vary widely. To outsiders, this seems almost mad, and trying to understand the rules that Waerds actually follow is often pointless. Despite this, the Wareds are oddly honorable among themselves and pragmatic about the lack of clear definitions. Each year, Wareds typically set aside specific times called the "Hunting" or the "Scouring." During the "Hunting", entire communities shift focus, dedicating themselves to long-season hunting trips. Families or communities venture into jungles to hunt monsters and creatures. During the "Scouring", the best warriors and hunters of the separate Bastions form semi-autonomous military units and engage in fierce skirmishes and battles between each other. While nearly all Wareds participate in these two annual periods, those living and working in bastions—engaged in trades, food production, or other professions—only undertake brief hunts or skirmishes, spending a few days a year in the jungles, wilderness, or battlefields instead of entire seasons.

Religion & Beliefs

While individuals Waerds recongise the Nineteen as a distant, all-encompassing Pantheron of deities with varying roles in society, they are almost fanatically devoted to the Shard God Lanespear. She is not a distant deity but a primal teacher of the spear and hunt who embodies the perfect hunter and slayer. Shrines to Lanespear are common and often referred to as Trophy Halls filled with preserved heads, colossal bones, thick scales, and calcified hearts of legendary beasts. For Waerds, a life without challenge lacks meaning, and avoiding or fearing to confront danger in any form is seen as the ultimate sin. They are highly pragmatic about death, and their culture holds little fear of dying, provided an individual accomplishes a great feat at least once in their life to prove themselves.

Clothing & Adornments

To outsiders, Waerds often appear as the very creatures they hunt. Their look is a patchwork of fur, scales, bones, hardened leathers, and delicately shaped metals that resemble claws or horns. Young Waerds usually wear little or no clothing until they start hunting independently, even as children, by returning with smaller creatures and learning to craft their own clothing. As they mature and defeat stronger enemies, they create armor and weapons from cured monster hides, chitinous plates, and sharp teeth. Beneath these extremly customized garments, Waerds also cover their bodies with ritualistic tattoos, viewing their skin as a record of their hunting and martial achievements. For many Waerds, protecting themselves with monster parts is just as important as leaving certain parts of their skin exposed to display their Ancestral Ink.

Cuisine & Diet

Among the Bastions, it is said that nothing is ever wasted. No kill is left to rot; every part has a purpose. This applies not only to weapons and armor but also to their industries and especially their food. Their diet is rich in meat from monsters and creatures they kill, prepared in a variety of complex dishes. Meats are heavily spiced, marinated, and then sautéed, grilled, deep-fried, boiled, or steamed. A popular delicacy is Marrow-Mash, a high-protein paste that is slowly cured, spiced with intense flavors, and served in hollowed-out monster horns.

Technology & Magic

Waerds generally dismiss most forms of magic. While they understand and respect the potency and power of wizards casting fireballs, they believe that such magic isn't very effective in many situations. Most mages are considered weak and unable to defend themselves in close combat. As a result, most Waerds view magic more as a supplement than a path to true power. Instead, they depend on the formidable strength of the numerous monsters and creatures in the Duskflare Jungles. If these creatures' scales, teeth, or bones hold magical properties, Waerds will gladly use them for their own use. The older a Waerd is, the more likely they are to have defeated powerful monsters and possess equipment, charms, or objects imbued with innate magic. Waerd technology appears quite basic at first glance—major Bastions are built from stone, but most villages, stones, or buildings are made from wood or large monster parts, and their technology advancement is glacial.

Social Structure & Government

The Waedrs are united by their beliefs and customs, rather than a single government or nationhood. In the Lowads, there are six major Bastions, with power shifting between these massive city-fortresses depending on which Bastion can claim more territory each season. Leadership is held by the six Euntwé, experienced veterans and elders, who are partly elected and have gained power through physical dominance. Their skin is almost entirely black with ink. Age is only one aspect of a Waerd's social standing, as it usually signifies experience and respect. However, an individual's skill and ability to defeat monsters are even more important. In rare cases, Waerds who have slain legendary monsters, such as dragons or Leviathans, are instantly promoted to leadership within their communities.

Those Waerds who have personally met Lanespear and earned her favor are called the Kinthyr. The Kinthyr stand apart from other Waerds in many ways. They are bestowed with wings and wear oddly ancient-looking armor adorned with glowing symbols that suggest a connection between the Waerds and Signara. Like their Mistress, they mediate the conflicts of the Lowlands, fighting for both sides. They also heal and restore fallen warriors and, in the event of a great warrior falling to monstrous incursions, carry their bodies back for veneration in fiery ceremonies.

Language & Communication

One of the most surprising aspects of Waerd culture is their language. Many assume it would be simple and limited, but in reality, it is incredibly complex, with more descriptive words than most other languages on Ember's surface. Words are spoken with refined, flowing elegance, making it considered a beautifully hypnotic tongue. They lack a standardized written system and instead use a combination of ancient glyphs passed down through their Ancestral Ink and pictograms carved into bark or trees, which guide other hunters in the wild.
Waerd.scoverview: The Waerds live on the subcontinent known as the Lowlands in southeastern Aterica; a humid region filled with putrid swamps, massive forests, and towering mountains infested with dragons. Waerds are not politically unified, but their culture is divided into several feuding strongholds that fight fierce battles and skirmishes. Although the political situation is quite chaotic, the Waerds see this as a backdrop to the real challenge: confronting, repelling, and hunting the monsters of the jungles to their north. They train from birth to kill all manner of deadly monsters and creatures, and over generations, they have become unparalleled slayers of unimaginable terrors.

Wardcall.name: Wardcall
Wardcall.text:
At a Glance

  • Language: [[/language borel]]

  • Capital City: @UUID[JournalEntry.xqx0clu8pT4kRxAz.JournalEntryPage.wlF44Ld4D2PqbR0v]{Ward'Kett}

  • Technology: Late bronze, early iron/steel production, Wardskin.

  • Major Religions/Beliefs: @UUID[JournalEntry.emberDeities0000.JournalEntryPage.wMAfwOrjwk0izpxC]{Auris Bor}, Trine of Wards

  • Names: Adante, Alenra, Althar, Djoran, Elith, Joren, Kareth, Kelthar, Korvic, Lorend, Mirok, Myrka, Nadra, Odan, Rathen, Rovana, Seraya, Sova, Talen, Tavric, Tysha, Valenne, Vasrik, Vaxen, Zel-Rathen

  • Ancestries: [[/ancestry emberKivahr]] (75%) + [[/ancestry emberKeth]] (5%), [[/ancestry emberHuman]] (5%) (Other @UUID[JournalEntry.emberAncestries0.JournalEntryPage.yc1bRBrDsyaIi2C6]{Ancestries} exist in small numbers).

The Frozen Oath

The Wardcall is the name given to a loose alliance of three kingdoms, Wintec, Katic, and Pertta, bound under the rule of High King Rathern Orian. Though outsiders often speak of the Wardcall as a single realm, its people rarely do. Wintarins, Katins, and Perttins are distinctly different in various subtle ways that outsiders often overlook, such as their regional accents and armor styles. It is considered deeply offensive to confuse someone with a member of another kingdom.

The people of the Wardcall are known for their restraint and ceremony, their strict sense of order, and their unshakable belief that endurance is a virtue above all others. To them, honor is not glory; it is survival. Much of their strength lies in the Ironfrost Templars, who hold the northern border keeps against the Vartic Clans, Skinchangers, and horrific monsters that roam beyond the Frostline. To many outside the Wardcall, they are the steadfast guardians of the north: disciplined, solemn, incorruptible. Yet those who have traveled their border towns and seen their forges at night speak differently.

The three kingdoms and the Ironfrost Templars have access to strange armor technology called Wardskin. This skin-tight armor covers the wearer completely up to the neck and hisses steam in the cold air. How it is made is not openly spoken of, though the process is said to take place in the Machinarims, temples of fire and steam that outsiders are forbidden to enter. There are stories, half-remembered and quickly dismissed, that the forges of the Wardcall burn hotter than metal alone can sustain.

Forty-three years have passed since Blood Binding, which saw the Wardcall region ripped apart in a bloody civil war and raised Rathern Orian to his throne. His victory ended the feuds of the old kings and border barons, and his peace has held since, but only barely. As the High King ages, questions of succession draw old tensions to the surface once more. The border keeps are restless. The temples to the Trine of Wards whisper, and the sharp blades so often turned north towards the monsters and Skinchangers may soon turn inward again.

The Wardcall’s official faith, the Trine of Wards, claims absolute religious authority across the three kingdoms. Its hidden temples, the Machinarims, dominate both the spiritual and industrial life of the north, where the sacred and the mechanical are bound together. Ward Clerics oversee every ritual and sermon, patrolling towns, keeps, and cities to root out doubt and deviation. Their presence is constant, watchful eyes beneath iron masks, ensuring obedience through faith and fear. Yet the Trine’s dominion is far from complete. Across the frozen lands, many still whisper prayers to the Gods of the @UUID[JournalEntry.emberDeities0000.JournalEntryPage.wMAfwOrjwk0izpxC]{Auris Bor}, the ancient pantheon of the north, and their forebears, the Bejak. Among these, @UUID[JournalEntry.emberDeities0000.JournalEntryPage.pEeJhnepW0PzeN9X]{Themis} is one of the few @UUID[JournalEntry.emberDeities0000.JournalEntryPage.6pJu6l3a7RTzcaRM]{Shard Gods} still spoken of, though never publicly worshipped. To the Trine, Themis is a dangerous influence, inspiring vigilante acts and personal vendettas under the guise of divine judgment.

Related Cultures

Historically, the Wardcall kingdoms were founded by a series of @UUID[JournalEntry.emberCultures000.JournalEntryPage.A1uPGhtaDifW8Sph]{Bejak} Kivahr families who traveled east into the snowy mountains. Despite the historical link, the harsh winters and fear of monsters have molded the Wardcall into a very different culture from the Bejak, and they maintain a distance that is only bridged by shared trade. In all, the Wardcall have few friends that they can rely upon nearby which forces a degree of isolation.
Wardcall.scoverview: The Wardcall is a loose alliance of three northern kingdoms, Wintec, Katic, and Pertta, united under High King Rathern Orian. Known for their discipline, honor, and martial traditions, the Wardcall appear as steadfast guardians of the Frostline, yet beneath their disciplined exterior lie whispered horrors, secretive temples, and the mysterious creation of Wardskin armor. Forty-three years after a brutal civil war known as the Blood Binding, the region remains tense, with old rivalries simmering beneath a fragile peace.
Wardcall.sgamemaster:
Outwardly, the Wardcall presents itself as a unified kingdom; they are disciplined, stoic, and martial, defending their northern borders from monsters and raiders. Beneath this veneer, however, the Wardcall are harsh, brutal, and unforgiving. They hunt Skinchangers without mercy, turning their bodies, blood, and bones into Wardskin armor, weapons, and talismans. Their hidden temple forges, known as Machinarims, are kept secret from outsiders, where Clerics of the Trine employ fire, steam, and blood rituals, blending faith, engineering, and unholy craft. Survival, duty, and obedience dominate life just as betrayal, hunger, and violence lurk beneath the surface. Political tension simmers constantly, and old rivalries from the Blood Binding civil war continue to shape every corner of society. The Wardcall is a culture of extremes: unyielding guardians above, ruthless predators below.

All three kingdoms of the Wardcall possess access to the deadly armor technology known as Wardskin. This skin-tight suit covers the wearer completely up to the neck and is typically worn beneath larger plates and helmets in settlements or during rest, giving the illusion of mundane protection. In war or when hunting monsters, it is stripped down to its base layer, becoming a streamlined and ruthlessly functional instrument of survival. Wardskin is almost always black, veined with thin lines of red and crimson, reinforced with armored guards along the arms, legs, and shoulders, and capped with a strange metallic spine along the back. In extreme cold, it can keep its wearer warm, venting steam around the neck, but this comfort comes at a cost. Extended use can cause severe overheating, excruciating pain, and even death.

Kessian.name: Kessian
Kessian.text:
At a Glance

  • Language: [[/language solical]]

  • Great City: @UUID[JournalEntry.xqx0clu8pT4kRxAz.JournalEntryPage.BYvYIdN1bQH4UIvR]{Kasarain}

  • Technology: Late bronze, early iron/steel production, enhanced with Sun magic.

  • Major Religions/Beliefs: @UUID[JournalEntry.emberDeities0000.JournalEntryPage.6cMQOhdBouTFJlSl]{Sunalins}

  • Names: Amara, Azizi, Bako, Bek-Zun, Chike, Daba, Enzor, Fola, Gidado, Helon, Ishe, Kaelo, Kazi, Kebe, Khorshi, Kwesi, Luan, Mazi, Nekun, Nyoka, Obasi, Olon, Oro, Phiri, Ra-Kesh, Sango, Solu, Tanza, Thabo, Udo, Vonne, Xola, Zun.

  • Ancestries: [[/ancestry emberHuman]] (65%) + [[/ancestry emberNirae]] (15%) (Other @UUID[JournalEntry.emberAncestries0.JournalEntryPage.yc1bRBrDsyaIi2C6]{Ancestries} exist in small numbers).

Sun Worshippers

The Kessian realm is a land of sun-drenched temples and ancient secrets. Long before The Shattering Humanity emerged upon the Aran Peninsula and began spreading across the world, in small bands and families, seeking new opportunities known as the Human Migrations. Before the Shattering, the Aedir fully supported the Humans' drive to expand, at least at first, and even helped them in various ways. One such way was settling the northern coast of the continent of Kasi (the ancient Aedir name for Kessia). This aid meant that for a long time, the Aedir played a crucial role in the development of the early Kessian settlements, and many Aedir lived and worked alongside Humans. After the Shattering, many of the Aedir who survived integrated into the flourishing Kessian culture.

In the aftermath of the Shattering, the Kessians began to worship Lantyr above all others, which evolved into daily rituals and ceremonies dedicated to honoring the sun and seeking her blessings. Kessians have also mastered harnessing solar energy to power their technology and sustain their way of life in the harsh desert environment. In Kessia, society follows a distinctly matriarchal structure; women are naturally regarded as leaders and governors. While Kessians are very proud of this social tendency, they continue to face ongoing issues with equality and have implemented various reforms and laws aimed at addressing ingrained biases.

Kessians reside in a region that was deeply affected by the Shattering; the once-glowing jungle colonies of the Aedir were wiped out and completely destroyed across what is now known as the Obsidian Desert. To this day, the Kessians live with the aftermath of that destruction, and as abyssal energy swirls and monsters emerge from the red sands and obsidian monoliths at the continent's center, they have little choice but to oppose them. For thousands of years, Kessians have stood resolutely against the Abyss, actively containing the spread of corruption, and they have become highly skilled at detecting and fighting it. While Kessians directly combat the Abyssal influence from the Obsidian Desert, they also fight its invasive and harmful effects on their people, often taking extreme measures. Some see their inquisitorial methods as excessive, but they are necessary for society's survival, and their relentless pursuit of corruption has continued as long as the Obsidian Desert has existed.

Related Cultures

The Kessians live upon a harsh and uncompromising continent, with a deep ocean separating them from most of the known world to the north. Despite this, the Kessians are excellent sailors and navigators and have strong ties to many cultures, including the Kelmezians and the Lumek, both of which are similar in many aspects culturally. The Lumek especially view Kessians as distant family, and the two peoples often help one another in times of crisis, and the Kessians have fielded an expeditionary force to help the Lumek against the undead Blood Barons for nearly 800 years.
Kessian.scoverview: Far to the south of the Aterican supercontinent is the radiant continent of Kessia, so named for the Kessian people who stand as a bulwark against the encroaching Obsidian Desert and have thrived in the unrelenting sun for thousands of years. Kessians are deeply rooted in traditions dating back to the Aedir Empire and they are fiercely protective of the cultural beliefs and ideas, most of which revolve around their devotion to Lantyr, the Sun.

Kelmezian.name: Kelmezian
Kelmezian.text:
At a Glance

  • Language: [[/language arcden]]

  • Great City: @UUID[JournalEntry.xqx0clu8pT4kRxAz.JournalEntryPage.HN2Zimps4w5XniZe]{Old Carinth}

  • Technology: Iron production, enhanced with stagnant technology

  • Major Religions/Beliefs: The @UUID[JournalEntry.emberDeities0000.JournalEntryPage.SXks9PsVzNyIPuDH]{Tanir}

  • Names: Aknos, Amantius, Amenos, Anubos, Basilikhes, Belisaros, Cassandur, Cyrusis, Eudoxor, Gennadios, Housis, Imotepos, Khenti, Komnenos, Leontios, Nepheris, Nikephor, Onnois, Osis-Vax, Pakhomios, Polemos, Razul, Sesostris, Tausertis, Tiberios, Xenothis, Zoseris.

  • Ancestries: Ancestries: [[/ancestry emberHuman]] (90%) (Other @UUID[JournalEntry.emberAncestries0.JournalEntryPage.yc1bRBrDsyaIi2C6]{Ancestries} exist in small numbers)

Ancient Urbanites

The Kelmezian City States are ancient, towering cities that spread across the badlands and deserts of south-west Aterica. It is believed that many of these cities were once the original settlements of Humanity, and before that, the ancestral homes of the Jarn clans. Today, these cities are old, chaotic urban environments where technology from hundreds or even thousands of years ago remains in active use. Jurimax Engineers tirelessly work to keep the cities functioning, though often in a futile, never-ending effort. The term Kelmezian has become more common in recent years, but residents strongly identify with their city of birth, from the crumbling factories of Old Carinth to the water-covered canals of Varena. To support their incredibly dense populations, the cities have perfected vertical agriculture through massive artificial farms, silos, and estates that pulse with life deep within the urban landscape. This dense urban density is managed by a complex network of noble factions, senates, and councils, all of whom must balance the grandeur of their towers against the crumbling, often abandoned lower levels.

The potential for overwhelming chaos and crime in such packed environments is held in check by the Nightwatch, an organization that operates with a fervor that borders on the fanatical. The Nightwatch are the true masters of the Kelmezian cities, with a unified command structure across every city in the region, and as their agents free-run across rooftops and through the shadowed underlayers, they hunt their criminal targets with relentless precision. In most Kelmezian cities, the Nightwatch is authorized to use deadly force, making them the singular, terrifying pillar of order in an otherwise lawless society.

The Kelmezian culture has become more unified recently due to the looming war with the Tayan Empire. The city of Yarinu has already fallen, lying in ruins that the Tayans use as a supply depot, while the people of Kalaxa are forced to abandon their homes as the front lines draw closer. This existential threat has forced a grim transformation as the ancient cities have slowly pivoted their industries towards war production. In addition, it's claimed that the Kelmezian 43rd Corp, holding the Tayan 2nd army at bay in the east, is actually winning and pushing back the invaders, which has sparked a massive upsurge in cultural identity and pride.

Related Cultures

The Kelmezian City States currently border two openly hostile cultures, the Railen in the south, where tensions are set to explode at any moment and the active war with the Tayan Empire to the north. This has caused a seismic shift in its relations with other cultures around the world as the Kelmezians desperately search for allies and support. The Mazirans across the Crossing Sea would make a natural alliance, as they are also under attack by the Tayan Empire, but unfortunately, they are divided amongst themselves. The Lumek believe the Tayan Empire is expanding only to secure a better future for people generally and they have no desire to enrage a nation that may one day be in a strong position to help them combat the Blood Barons. Thus, the Kelmezians find themselves isolated and solely responsible, at least for now, for halting the expansion of the Tayan Empire.
Kelmezian.scoverview: The Kelmezian City states are among the oldest edifices of Humanity, dating back to before the Shattering, and in the present age, they are each colossal settlements of immense grandeur, from glimmering towers to darkened corners of the underlayers. While each city is unique and citizens typically refer to their city of birth rather than calling themselves "Kelmezian" they share many similarities that bind them together.

Railen.name: Railen
Railen.text:
At a Glance

  • Language: [[/language scripta]]

  • Great City: @UUID[JournalEntry.xqx0clu8pT4kRxAz.JournalEntryPage.m4UyLxbFrbiONIb8]{Ancalen}

  • Technology: Late Medieval, Ancient Luxaran light magic.

  • Major Religions/Beliefs: The Triarchy

  • Names: Adrax, Adrel, Antaka, Astrax, Brill-Vark, Illum, Ilmak, Ilu-Rahl, Kor-Vax, Korrak, Lorche, Lorek, Lucos-Kar, Lukant, Mastte, Min-Xul, Rael-Toth, Sarka, Tal-Karn, Vax-Adel, Vial.

  • Ancestries: [[/ancestry emberAltyra]] (95%) + (Other @UUID[JournalEntry.emberAncestries0.JournalEntryPage.yc1bRBrDsyaIi2C6]{Ancestries} exist in small numbers).

Zealous Conquerors

Martial power, strength, and displays of fighting prowess are highly respected traits among the Railen, who are a highly homogeneous society; they are taught from birth to revere cultural isolation. The Railen express a deep sense of superiority over other cultures and a strong belief that their ideas and way of life are the greatest in the entire world. However, there is some small amount of ancestral diversity within the culture, with humans and other ancestors of various cultural backgrounds present in Ancalen. And despite these other ancestries being treated as second-class citizens in many cases, the Railen people are not outwardly or obviously bigoted. Instead, Altyran Railen are provided more respect and positions of authority in governance, military, and commerce. Many Railen owe this privilege to a deep, nearly sub-conscious belief that their connection to Luxarum — and the Light of the Tyraphem has given the Altyran people greater abilities along with the very responsibility to achieve greatness.

The Ekat is a group of one hundred of the most powerful members of Ancalen society, and are easily recognized by the enchanted armor they wear, known as Lightplates. These Lightplates are a singular relic split among the one hundred Ekat users. In preparation for their inevitable death, a Lightplate wearer will do everything possible to "retire" their armor and pass it to the next worthy warrior. Lightplates are smooth, clean, and seamless in appearance, which gives the Ekat members an almost otherworldly quality while wearing them. Lightplates are also marked with designs that clearly state the wearer's current rank among the Ekat. It's understood that the Lightplates were a gift from the Tyraphem of Luxaraum at some point (at least, the Railen themselves suspeect this is the case). The only way to advance among the Ekat ranks is to defeat a member at a higher rank; and while such clashes are rarely deadly among lower tiers of Ekat, higher-rank conflicts are intense, brutal, and occasionally deadly.

The most powerful members of Railen culture are the Triarcs — Szure, Tazarl, and Lucon — the three highest-ranking members of the Ekat and the principal rulers of the Luminous City. In reality, the Triarcs are all Shard Gods, siblings that ascended together somewhat recently (around six hundred years ago) and have been solely responsible for guiding the Ancalen culture ever since. In addition to their martial strength, each member of the Triarchy is also worshiped by Railen society, as they represent the pinnacle of their militaristic traditions and cultural beliefs.
Railen.scoverview: The Railen are a strict, intolerant, and militaristic people from the Aran Peninsula comprised almost entirely of humanoids descended from Altyra ancestry. This haughty and headstrong culture hails from the Luminous City of Ancalen, the birthplace of Humanity, which is considered by many to be one of the Ember's greatest cities. The Railen are a rather homogeneous people who tend to hold similar beliefs, traditions, and goals. Aside from their strict adherence to the religious doctrine of the Triarchy, the most important aspect of Railen society is an individual or organization's martial prowess, and they respect strength in many different forms — be it military, resources, socio-political influence, or raw might.

Fikost.name: Fikost
Fikost.text:
At a Glance

  • Language: [[/language kost]]

  • Great City: @UUID[JournalEntry.xqx0clu8pT4kRxAz.JournalEntryPage.UeziKENAQNnY5lYj]{Rimedrift}

  • Technology: Symbiotic with nature, enhanced with Ice magic, Living Shipbuilding

  • Major Religions/Beliefs: @UUID[JournalEntry.emberDeities0000.JournalEntryPage.wMAfwOrjwk0izpxC]{Auris Bor}

  • Names:Drenak, Jorua, Keleno, Kethun, Mako, Makren, Moroa, Orilo, Otikai, Ramar, Rautan, Solten, Tavake, Tevak, Tolai, Toruan, Torenka, Vaoro, Varu, Vekai.

  • Ancestries: [[/ancestry emberWirrun]] (95%) (Other @UUID[JournalEntry.emberAncestries0.JournalEntryPage.yc1bRBrDsyaIi2C6]{Ancestries} exist in small numbers).

Driftborn Nomads

Far in the frozen reaches of the north dwell the Fikost, the merciless hunters of the deep and masters of the icebound seas. Made up almost entirely of the Wirrun, few other Ancestries can endure the killing cold this far north, and even the hardy @UUID[JournalEntry.emberAncestries0.JournalEntryPage.0YvoRkcs1BxtRiQz]{Vrjnhar} must rely on thick furs and enchanted warming stones to survive. The Fikost, however, are a culture shaped entirely by a hostile world; their culture, faith, and very blood honed by centuries of enduring the icy wastes and an endless winter.

The Fikost way of life is built upon the hunt. They stalk the colossal beasts that roam the Hoarfrost Sea and the frozen plains that surround them on the continent of @UUID[JournalEntry.xqx0clu8pT4kRxAz.JournalEntryPage.UXitezaq69A5JVmd]{Aterica}, from massive schools of razor-toothed fish to the great Whalufa and even @UUID[JournalEntry.emberBestiary000.JournalEntryPage.OPfBWA2N4EY974Wi]{Leviathans} and darker horrors that dwell in the deep. Their skill at drawing such creatures to the surface is unmatched, blending powerful sea-magic that can lure or bind what no ordinary line or net could hold.

Unlike most peoples of Aterica, the Fikost do not have any true settlements upon the mainland. Instead, they live aboard vast living ships, semi-sentient vessels grown from enchanted ice, bones, and Deepstrand. These ships are tended like kin, fed and maintained over generations, their hulls singing in low, mournful tones as they drift through the polar mists. Each has its own temperament, slow and cold-minded, yet fiercely loyal to its crew. A ship may choose its captain, bond with its family, and even refuse to sail if dishonored or wronged. To lose a ship is to lose a treasured friend and Fikost mourn such losses as they would the death of a family member.

The Fikost often hunt the tundra and the frigid depths alike, bringing their kills back to their floating ships anchored along the ice-sheathed coast. The mainland itself is too perilous as packs of monstrous Trolls, Abyssal monsters, and Mur’kaal roam the wastes, slaughtering all they find. The Fikost despise the Trolls, yet they are too pragmatic to fight them openly. They know that large-scale slaughter of Trolls can trigger explosive breeding cycles an old, grim truth passed down through generations. Thus, the Fikost avoid conflict when they can, vanish into blizzards and the icy seas.

Related Cultures

The Fikost trade with the @UUID[JournalEntry.emberCultures000.JournalEntryPage.A1uPGhtaDifW8Sph]{Bejak} to their south and have a warm and friendly relationship, based on mutual respect and a combined hatred and fear of @UUID[JournalEntry.emberBestiary000.JournalEntryPage.t0uXEiiy4hN4XBeX]{Trolls}. The Fikost somewhat ignore the vicious Vartic Clans that live in the cold mountains to their east, though remarkably, trade between the two peoples is not uncommon.
